unit.name: The Roman Army & the Values of War
unit.subtitle: The Roman war machine - the legion and the legionary, arms, armour and the marching camp, Roman campaigns, and the ideals of heroism and leadership in war.

lessons.title: The Roman Legion
lessons.description: How the Roman legion was structured, trained and disciplined into the ancient world's most formidable army.
lessons.content_html:
The Backbone of Roman Power

At the heart of Rome’s empire lay an extraordinary military machine. The legion was not simply a fighting force — it was the engine of conquest, colonisation and control. Understanding how the legion was organised tells us a great deal about Roman values: discipline, hierarchy, collective identity, and the expectation that citizens owed military service to the state.

Recruitment and the Citizen-Soldier

In the Imperial period, legionaries were Roman citizens who signed up for a standard term of twenty-five years. Recruits had to be physically fit, of free birth, and free from serious criminal convictions. Provincial men who were not yet citizens could serve in auxiliary units, and on completion of service they were rewarded with Roman citizenship. This arrangement meant the army was also a powerful mechanism for spreading Roman identity across the empire.

Pay was a key incentive. Legionaries received a regular salary, a share of campaign booty, and a substantial land grant or cash payment on discharge. These rewards tied the soldier’s loyalty directly to the general who commanded him — a fact that had enormous political consequences throughout Roman history.

Key Fact

A Roman legion was divided into ten cohorts. Each cohort contained six centuries of around eighty men. Each century was commanded by a centurion — the most important officer in the Roman army’s day-to-day operation.

The Structure of the Legion

The legion’s genius lay in its modular structure. At the top was the legionary legate, a senior senator appointed by the emperor. Below him, six tribunes assisted with administration. The real fighting backbone, however, was the centurion. A centurion was identified by three distinctive features: a transverse crest (crista transversa) on his helmet, a vine stick (vitis) used both as a symbol of authority and an instrument of punishment, and his gladius worn on the left hip — the reverse of ordinary legionaries, who wore theirs on the right. The most senior centurion in a legion, the primus pilus, was a figure of immense prestige.

The first cohort was larger than the rest, containing five double-strength centuries of around 160 men each, giving it a total strength of roughly 800 soldiers. It was the pride of the legion and typically held the position of greatest honour in battle.

At the symbolic heart of every legion stood the aquila — a golden eagle mounted on a staff. The eagle was carried by the aquilifer, one of the most honoured soldiers in the unit. To lose the aquila in battle was one of the greatest disgraces a Roman army could suffer. When three legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus were destroyed in the Teutoburg Forest in 9 AD, the recovery of their lost eagles became a national obsession pursued for decades. The bronze statuette of a legionary held in the British Museum (1867, 0510.4) shows the typical equipment of an Imperial soldier and gives us a vivid material record of how these men looked when on parade.

Training and Discipline

Roman training was systematic and relentless. New recruits practised weapons techniques against a wooden post called a palus, using weapons that were deliberately heavier than standard issue so that the real thing would feel lighter in battle. Soldiers were expected to march twenty Roman miles in five hours in full armour and kit, and to be capable of constructing a fully defended camp at the end of that march.

Discipline was enforced with brutal efficiency. Infractions were punished by flogging; sleeping on duty could mean death. The ultimate collective punishment was decimation, in which one man in ten from a disgraced unit was chosen by lot to be beaten to death by his comrades. Though rarely used, its existence shaped the psychological climate of the legion. This culture of iron discipline had been celebrated in Roman literature for centuries before the Imperial period, and it was seen as a defining national virtue.

Key Fact

Roman legionaries were professional soldiers paid a regular wage. They trained in close-order fighting, engineering and camp-building. The bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum is a key material source for understanding their standard equipment during the Imperial period.

The Greek hoplite phalanx depended on citizen-farmers who owned their own equipment and served for limited seasonal campaigns. The Roman legion, by contrast, was a permanent professional army whose soldiers trained full-time and served for decades. Roman soldiers were also engineers: they could bridge rivers, build siege engines and construct fortified camps, giving the army a strategic flexibility no phalanx could match. Roman legionary coins, such as the Mark Antony Legionary denarius — minted around 32 BC with a galley on one face and an eagle between two standards on the other — were literally struck by generals to pay their troops, showing how tightly military identity and payment were bound together in the Roman system.

The Legionary Fortress

When a legion was stationed in a province, it occupied a permanent legionary fortress. The fortress at Chester (Deva) in Britain is one of the best-preserved examples and is listed as a prescribed material source. A typical fortress was a large rectangular enclosure with a regular internal layout: the headquarters building (principia) at the centre, the commanding officer’s house (praetorium) beside it, barracks blocks for each century arranged in rows, granaries, a hospital and a bathhouse. This regularity — the same layout wherever in the empire a fortress was built — reinforced Roman identity and made it easier for soldiers to function efficiently even in unfamiliar surroundings.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When you are asked to ‘describe’ the structure of the Roman army, give specific terminology: legion, cohort, century, centurion, aquila. Avoid vague phrases like “lots of soldiers were organised into groups.” When a source question shows the bronze legionary statuette or the Legionary denarius, use specific details you can see or know about the object — its material, what it shows, where it was found or minted. The examiner’s most common criticism is that students describe sources only in general terms rather than analysing their specific features.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A Roman legion comprised roughly 5,000 citizen-soldiers divided into ten cohorts, each of six centuries commanded by a centurion; the first cohort was the largest and most prestigious.
  • Legionaries were long-service professionals, paid regularly and rewarded with a pension; discipline was severe and the loss of the eagle standard (aquila) was the army’s greatest disgrace.
  • Material sources — including the bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum and the Roman fortress at Chester — give direct evidence for how the legion was equipped and housed.

practice_questions.text: Name the officer who commanded a century in the Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: centurion.

practice_questions.text: Describe the standard structure of a Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three, for example: a legion contained roughly 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers; it was divided into ten cohorts; each cohort was made up of six centuries of around eighty men; each century was commanded by a centurion; the first cohort was double-strength and held the place of greatest honour.

practice_questions.text:
Read this description of a Roman material source: a small bronze statuette, approximately 8 cm tall, showing a soldier standing in a relaxed pose. He wears segmented body armour over a tunic, carries a large rectangular shield, and on his head sits a helmet with cheek-guards. A short sword hangs from his right hip. The figure was found in Britain and is now in the British Museum (1867, 0510.4).

What does this source tell us about the Roman legionary in the Imperial period? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of specific features of the source (armour, shield, sword, helmet) linked to wider knowledge of the legion's equipment and organisation. The response considers what the source confirms and what it cannot tell us (e.g. it shows parade or off-duty dress, not necessarily battle formation). At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details from the source, linked to accurate knowledge of the legionary's role. Some consideration of what the source reveals or limits.
Developing: General reference to the source with limited specific detail; knowledge of the legion mainly descriptive.
Emerging: Minimal engagement with the source; knowledge vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why training and discipline were important to the success of the Roman legion.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: rigorous weapons training meant soldiers could fight effectively in close order; heavy training weapons meant real equipment felt lighter in battle; the ability to march twenty miles and then build a camp gave the army strategic flexibility; severe punishments (flogging, decimation) maintained collective discipline and prevented cowardice; standardised training meant soldiers from different parts of the empire could fight together effectively.

practice_questions.text: How useful is the Roman fortress at Chester as evidence for understanding the Roman army in the Imperial period?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis weighing the site's specific strengths (regular layout revealing hierarchy and function, barracks showing how centuries were housed, presence of hospital and bathhouse indicating permanent settlement) against limitations (the site has been altered over time; we cannot know the day-to-day experience of soldiers from the architecture alone). Named features of the site are used precisely.
Secure: Clear discussion of what the fortress reveals, with some acknowledgement of limitations. Specific features are named.
Developing: Mainly descriptive account of the fortress with limited evaluative comment.
Emerging: Vague reference to the fortress; limited accurate knowledge.

practice_questions.text: How important was discipline to the Roman army? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that evaluates discipline as central to Roman military effectiveness, supported by specific evidence (training with the palus, punishment by flogging, decimation as collective terror, the aquila as a symbol demanding collective commitment). The response also considers discipline alongside other factors (professional pay and rewards, engineeering skills, modular organisation) and reaches a supported judgement on the relative importance of discipline. Named sources are integrated.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Some range of points; a supported conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points about discipline but limited range; explanation may be underdeveloped or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited or missing; may retell facts without argument.

lessons.title: Arms, Armour & the Camp
lessons.description: The legionary's weapons, armour and the remarkable Roman marching camp that protected the army on campaign.
lessons.content_html:
Equipped to Conquer

A Roman legionary in the Imperial period was one of the best-equipped soldiers in the ancient world. His weapons and armour were the product of centuries of refinement, shaped by hard experience in wars against enemies who fought in very different ways. Understanding the legionary’s kit connects directly to understanding how Rome fought and won an empire — and the material evidence for this equipment survives in sculptures, coins, and the objects themselves.

Offensive Weapons: the Gladius and Pilum

The legionary’s primary weapon was the gladius. Unlike Greek or Celtic swords designed for slashing, the gladius was a short, double-edged weapon used primarily for thrusting. In the close press of battle, where there was no room for wide swings, a short stabbing sword was devastatingly effective. The gladius gave the legionary a decisive advantage once the enemy’s formation had been broken.

Before closing with the sword, the legionary threw a heavy javelin known as the pilum. The pilum was a remarkable piece of engineering: a wooden shaft with a long iron shank topped by a small pyramidal head. The iron shank was deliberately thin so that it would bend or snap on impact, wedging into the enemy’s shield and weighing it down. Even if the pilum did not wound its target, the stricken shield became a liability that the enemy had to discard before he could fight effectively. A volley of pila delivered just before the charge created shock, disorder and disadvantage in the opposing line.

Key Fact

The legionary fought with three weapons in sequence: the pilum (heavy javelin thrown to disrupt the enemy line), the gladius (short stabbing sword for close combat), and a pugio (dagger for last resort). Each weapon served a specific tactical purpose in the Roman system of fighting.

Defensive Equipment: Shield and Armour

The legionary’s large rectangular shield, the scutum, was one of his most important pieces of equipment. In the Imperial period, the scutum was typically semi-cylindrical in shape, curving around the soldier’s body to protect his left side. Made from layers of wood glued at right angles (a technique similar to modern plywood), covered in leather and linen, with a metal boss at the centre, it was both strong and relatively lightweight. The boss could be used offensively to punch and knock opponents off balance.

The body was protected by lorica segmentata. This articulated armour was constructed from overlapping strips of iron plate, connected by leather straps and brass fittings. It was flexible enough to allow the wearer to move, crouch and fight, yet strong enough to deflect sword cuts and arrows. The head was protected by a close-fitting iron helmet with a neckguard, cheekpieces and a brow-plate to deflect downward blows. The bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum gives a clear visual record of how these elements combined in the soldier’s overall appearance.

The combination of pilum, gladius and scutum was designed to produce a specific fighting method. Soldiers advanced in close formation, locked shields to form a wall, threw their pila at the last moment, then pushed into the disordered enemy with their gladii. The tortoise formation (testudo) showed the scutum’s versatility: used during sieges, soldiers locked shields above their heads and on all sides to create a near-impenetrable shell against arrows and thrown stones. The equipment and the tactics were inseparable — remove one element and the whole system was weakened.

The Marching Camp

One of the most remarkable things about the Roman army was not what it did in battle but what it built every single night on campaign. The Roman marching camp was a fully fortified enclosure constructed at the end of each day’s march. Vegetius, writing in the late Roman period, describes the procedure clearly: the camp had a standard rectangular layout, with gates on all four sides, a rampart and ditch on the perimeter, and a regular internal arrangement of tents and streets that meant every soldier knew exactly where to go.

The rampart was built from the earth dug out of the surrounding ditch. The ditch was V-shaped, typically around 1.5 metres wide and approximately 0.9 metres deep (five Roman feet wide and three Roman feet deep, as described by the military writer Vegetius), making it difficult to cross under fire. On top of the rampart, soldiers planted sharpened stakes that they carried as part of their standard marching kit. This combination of ditch, rampart and stakes created a defensible perimeter in just a few hours. The ability to fortify a position every night meant a Roman army could never be caught completely unprepared by a night attack — a huge strategic advantage.

Key Fact

The Roman marching camp was a temporary fortified enclosure built every evening on campaign. It had a rectangular layout, a perimeter ditch, a rampart built from the excavated earth, and sharpened stakes on top. The Roman fortress at Chester grew out of this temporary camp tradition into a permanent installation.

Roman engineering extended to siege warfare. When faced with a fortified town, the legion could construct a full siege complex: approach ramps of earth and timber, artillery platforms for ballistae (bolt-throwing machines) and onagri (stone-throwing catapults), and covered corridors to advance soldiers under missile fire. Trajan’s Column in Rome, which depicts the emperor’s campaigns against the Dacians in the early second century AD, is a richly detailed carved relief running in a spiral around the column shaft. Among its many scenes are soldiers building camps, bridging rivers, operating artillery and conducting assaults — making it one of the most comprehensive visual sources we have for Roman military practice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Source analysis questions often present a material source such as the bronze legionary statuette or an extract from Trajan’s Column. You must use specific details from the source — for the statuette, mention the segmented armour, the shield boss, the helmet design; for Trajan’s Column, mention the spiral narrative format, the scene type (building, fighting, parading) and what it reveals about Roman values. Vague responses that simply describe “a soldier in armour” without engaging with the source’s specific features will score in the lower bands.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Roman legionary fought with pilum (thrown to disorder the enemy), gladius (short stabbing sword) and scutum (large curved shield), protected by lorica segmentata; each weapon was designed for a specific tactical purpose.
  • The marching camp — a fortified rectangular enclosure built every night on campaign — gave Rome a huge strategic advantage; the permanent fortress at Chester evolved from this tradition.
  • Key material sources include the bronze legionary statuette in the British Museum and Trajan’s Column, which together give detailed visual evidence for Roman military equipment and practice.

practice_questions.text: Give two weapons carried by a Roman legionary into battle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct weapon up to two: gladius (short stabbing sword); pilum (heavy javelin); pugio (dagger). Accept accurate description if exact term not given.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Roman scutum and explain its importance in battle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three: the scutum was a large rectangular or semi-cylindrical shield; it was made from laminated wood covered in leather and linen; it curved around the soldier's body to protect his left side; the central metal boss could be used offensively to punch opponents; it was used collectively to form the testudo formation in sieges.

practice_questions.text:
Look at this description of a Roman material source: a tall marble column standing in Rome, decorated with a continuous spiral relief carving. The relief depicts scenes from a military campaign: soldiers constructing a camp by digging a ditch and piling up earth; legionaries marching in formation; artillery machines being operated; a commander addressing his troops from a platform.

What does this source tell us about the Roman army? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis linking specific scene types (camp building, formation marching, artillery use, commander speech) to wider knowledge of Roman military practice. The response considers the source's purpose (imperial propaganda glorifying Trajan) alongside what it reveals, and acknowledges its limitations (official version, not a neutral record). At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details from the source with accurate supporting knowledge. Some engagement with what the source reveals and what it might not show.
Developing: General reference to the source; mainly descriptive; limited analytical comment.
Emerging: Minimal engagement; knowledge vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pilum was such an effective weapon against enemy formations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: the pilum's long iron shank bent on impact, preventing the enemy from throwing it back; if it hit a shield, the bent shaft weighed the shield down, forcing the enemy to drop it; this left the opponent exposed just before the Romans closed with their gladii; a simultaneous volley of pila from a century created shock and disorder in the enemy line at the critical moment.

practice_questions.text: How effective was Roman military equipment in giving the legionary an advantage over his enemies?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis covering multiple pieces of equipment (pilum, gladius, scutum, lorica segmentata) and explaining precisely how each gave a tactical advantage. The response also considers limitations (enemy adaptations, terrain limitations) and uses named sources. A supported conclusion is reached.
Secure: Clear argument covering at least two pieces of equipment with developed explanations. Mostly sustained.
Developing: Some relevant points but limited range or development.
Emerging: Simple descriptive points; limited argument.

practice_questions.text: How important was Roman engineering skill to military success? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument evaluating engineering as a core Roman military advantage, covering camp-building (daily fortification on campaign), siege equipment (ballistae, approach ramps), bridge-building, and the construction of permanent fortresses. The response sets this against other factors (equipment quality, unit discipline, tactical flexibility) and reaches a supported judgement. Named sources (Trajan's Column, Chester fortress, Vegetius) are integrated as evidence.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant evidence and sustained explanation. Some range of points and a supported conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant points; limited range or one-sided argument.
Emerging: Simple points; evidence limited; may retell without arguing.

lessons.title: Roman Warfare & Expansion
lessons.description: How Rome fought and won an empire — key campaigns, siege tactics and the battle of Actium that changed history.
lessons.content_html:
Rome at War

Rome did not acquire its empire by accident. Over five centuries of nearly continuous warfare, the Roman army developed and adapted tactics, organisation and technology that allowed it to defeat opponents as varied as Macedonian phalanxes, Celtic warbands, desert guerrillas and Eastern cavalry. This lesson focuses on Roman warfare in the Imperial period and on two key conflicts: Trajan’s campaigns against the Dacians in the early second century AD, and the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC that determined who would rule the Roman world.

Tactics and Adaptability

The Roman army’s greatest strength was its capacity to adapt. When facing enemies who excelled in archery, Rome recruited auxiliary archers from Syria. When fighting desert nomads, it reorganised supply lines. The fundamental tactical approach, however, was consistent: use the pilum volley to disorder the enemy, close to sword range, and overwhelm with disciplined pressure from the scutum-wall.

Roman generals understood that battle was often decided before it started — by choosing ground, by tiring the enemy, by cutting off supply lines. The logistics of a Roman campaign were extraordinary: granaries at fortresses along the Rhine and Danube, a network of roads that allowed rapid troop movements, and a river fleet that carried supplies deep into enemy territory. Trajan’s Column records this infrastructure vividly — among its carved scenes are soldiers unloading supplies from boats and engineers constructing pontoon bridges.

Key Fact

Trajan fought two major campaigns against the Dacians: the First Dacian War (101–102 AD) and the Second Dacian War (105–106 AD). Both are recorded in detail on Trajan’s Column in Rome and commemorated on the Arch of Trajan at Benevento — two of the most important prescribed visual sources for Roman warfare.

Trajan’s Dacian Campaigns

Dacia, roughly equivalent to modern Romania, was a powerful kingdom north of the Danube ruled by a capable king named Decebalus. Decebalus had humiliated Rome in previous conflicts, extracting tribute money and capturing Roman prisoners. Trajan invaded in 101 AD to recover Roman prestige and to seize Dacian gold reserves that were among the largest in the ancient world. The first war ended with Decebalus surrendering and agreeing to Roman terms; when he broke those terms, Trajan launched a second, more brutal campaign that ended with the destruction of the Dacian capital Sarmizegetusa and Decebalus’s suicide rather than capture.

Trajan’s Column, standing in Rome, is a hollow marble column roughly 30 metres tall, around whose shaft winds a continuous carved relief depicting both campaigns in over 150 individual scenes. The column begins with river-gods and troops crossing a pontoon bridge and moves through sieges, battle scenes, negotiations and triumphal processions to the final conquest. The Arch of Trajan at Benevento, a triumphal arch decorated with relief panels, shows Trajan receiving submission from Dacian enemies, distributing grain to Roman citizens, and associating his victories with divine favour. Both monuments present the campaigns as evidence of Roman greatness and Trajan’s exceptional leadership.

Trajan’s Column is an invaluable source for Roman military practice — it shows fort construction, river crossings, artillery use, allied auxiliary troops and siege operations in remarkable detail. However, it was a piece of state propaganda. Trajan is always shown in a commanding position; Roman soldiers are always disciplined and orderly. The Dacians are depicted as brave enemies to make the conquest more impressive, but they are also shown in defeat and submission. The column does not show Roman atrocities, looting or the suffering of civilian populations — it presents an idealised narrative of Roman power. Students must weigh this selectivity when using the column as evidence.

Siege Warfare

Roman success against fortified towns and hillfort strongholds depended on specialised siege techniques. The standard approach involved surrounding the enemy position with a circumvallation — a wall or ditch that encircled the entire position and cut off all resupply. This was then supplemented by direct assault: battering rams mounted in wheeled towers, artillery firing stones and bolts, and approach ramps of earth built up to the level of the enemy walls. Trajan’s Column shows all of these techniques in use against Dacian hillforts.

The Battle of Actium, 31 BC

The naval battle of Actium was fought off the coast of north-western Greece on 2 September 31 BC. On one side was Octavian (the future Augustus) commanding a fleet under his brilliant admiral Marcus Agrippa. On the other were the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII of Egypt. The battle decided who would control the entire Roman world. Octavian’s victory made him undisputed master of Rome and led directly to the establishment of the Roman Empire.

The trireme had been the dominant warship of the classical Greek period, but by Actium the principal warships were larger vessels called quinqueremes and triremes built on a grander scale. Agrippa’s fleet used grappling hooks and boarding tactics to neutralise Antony’s heavier ships. When Cleopatra’s squadron broke off the engagement and retreated towards Egypt, Antony followed — and his remaining fleet, left without leadership, surrendered. The battle showed that naval supremacy could decide the fate of an entire empire.

Key Fact

The battle of Actium (31 BC) saw Octavian’s fleet under Agrippa defeat the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. The victory is commemorated by a relief in the Vatican Museum and on the shield depicted on the Augustus of Prima Porta statue, where the scene of Actium is carved in miniature on the emperor’s breastplate armour.

The Romans invested enormous effort in commemorating military victory in permanent public form. Triumphal arches — like the Arch of Trajan at Benevento — were built at key road entry points so that every traveller would be reminded of Roman greatness. Victory columns like Trajan’s Column placed the narrative of a campaign literally at the heart of the city, in the forum that bore the emperor’s name. Coins were struck to broadcast the victory to every corner of the empire: the Mark Antony Legionary denarius (minted c. 32 BC) shows a warship on the obverse and an eagle between two military standards on the reverse, advertising his naval and military strength to his soldiers. Even defeat was commemorated: Augustus recovered the eagles lost by Varus in the Teutoburg Forest disaster (9 AD) decades later and displayed them publicly as proof that Rome always demanded and achieved satisfaction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering essay questions about Roman warfare and expansion, avoid simply listing battles and dates. The examiner wants you to argue — for example, arguing that engineering was more important than weapons, or that propaganda (Trajan’s Column, the Arch at Benevento) tells us as much about Roman values as about what actually happened. Use named sources as evidence for your argument, not just as decoration. Common pitfall: treating Trajan’s Column as a neutral record rather than as a monument designed to glorify the emperor.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Trajan fought two Dacian campaigns (101–102 AD and 105–106 AD); both are recorded on Trajan’s Column and the Arch of Trajan at Benevento, which are key prescribed visual sources presenting victories as imperial propaganda.
  • The battle of Actium (31 BC) saw Octavian’s fleet defeat Antony and Cleopatra, making Octavian master of the Roman world and leading to the creation of the Roman Empire under Augustus.
  • Roman military success rested on adaptable tactics, engineering capability (camps, siege works, roads) and the political use of commemorative monuments to project Roman power.

practice_questions.text: How useful is Trajan's Column as a source for understanding Roman military campaigns?

practice_questions.text: How effectively did Rome use both military force and propaganda to expand and maintain its empire? Use a range of evidence in your answer.

Mastering: A sustained argument evaluating both military effectiveness (tactics, engineering, siege warfare, adaptability) and the role of propaganda (Trajan's Column, the Arch at Benevento, coins, triumphal arches) in projecting and consolidating Roman power. The response argues that the two were inseparable — victory was worthless without commemoration, and propaganda without victory was hollow. Named sources are integrated throughout. A supported judgement is reached.
Secure: Clear argument covering both military and propaganda dimensions with relevant evidence. Some range and a supported conclusion.
Developing: Mostly covers one dimension (military or propaganda); limited engagement with the other.
Emerging: Simple points; largely descriptive; evidence thin.

lessons.title: Heroism & Leadership in War
lessons.description: What courage, glory and leadership meant in Greek and Roman war — from Leonidas and Tyrtaeus to Caesar and Virgil.
lessons.content_html:
The Ideal of the Warrior

In both Greek and Roman culture, the warrior was not simply a fighter — he was a moral exemplar. How a man behaved in battle was seen as the truest test of his character. The values associated with military heroism — courage, endurance, loyalty to comrades and willingness to die for one’s community — were celebrated in literature, memorialised in public monuments and held up as ideals that every free male citizen should aspire to. Understanding these values is essential for interpreting the literary and visual sources for warfare.

Greek Values of War: Honour and Shame

Greek war culture was built on the concepts of kleos (glory) and time (honour). A warrior who fought bravely and died well won kleos that would outlive him — his name would be remembered in song and story. A warrior who fled the field, discarded his shield, or surrendered brought lasting shame not only on himself but on his family and community. This culture of shame is expressed powerfully in the Spartan saying attributed to mothers sending sons to war: “Come back with your shield, or on it” — meaning either victorious or dead, but never in flight.

The Spartan poet Tyrtaeus expressed this value system with striking force. His Fragment 10, known as ‘The Fallen Warrior’, is one of the prescribed literary sources. In it, Tyrtaeus argues that dying in the front rank of battle is the finest thing a young man can do. He contrasts the eternal glory of the fallen warrior with the misery of the exile who wanders as a beggar, dishonoured and unwelcome everywhere. For Tyrtaeus, dying bravely for Sparta is not just admirable — it is the only thing that makes a life worthwhile. The poem was designed to be performed at syssitia (communal dining halls where Spartan soldiers ate and trained together), keeping the ideal of heroic self-sacrifice constantly present in the warrior community.

Key Fact

Tyrtaeus’s Fragment 10 (‘The Fallen Warrior’) is a Spartan poem that celebrates dying in battle as the highest honour. It contrasts the glory of the man who dies in the front rank with the shame and misery of the man who abandons his position. It was performed at Spartan communal meals to reinforce the warrior ideal.

Heroism at Thermopylae

The values expressed by Tyrtaeus found their most famous embodiment at the battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC. The Spartan king Leonidas and roughly three hundred Spartan warriors, along with several thousand allied troops, held the narrow mountain pass against the vast Persian army of Xerxes for three days. When the Spartan ally Ephialtes showed the Persians a path around the pass, Leonidas sent away the allied contingents and remained with his Spartans and a few Thespians and Thebans to fight to the death. According to Herodotus, when told that Persian arrows would blot out the sun, the Spartan Dienekes replied that they would fight in the shade. The defiant last stand became a defining moment of Greek identity — proof that courage and discipline could transform defeat into moral victory.

The prescribed visual source for Spartan warfare — the bronze warrior figure from the British Museum (1929, 1016.6) — is a small bronze statuette of a Spartan soldier, leaning forward slightly as if about to advance. It is simple and austere, perfectly matching the Spartan self-image: no decoration, no ostentation, just readiness for battle. This material source complements the literary portrait of Spartan heroism that we find in Tyrtaeus and Herodotus.

The Greeks marked the site at Thermopylae with an inscription that became famous throughout the ancient world. The verse, attributed to the poet Simonides, declared that the dead lay here in obedience to the words of Sparta. The inscription made the site a permanent reminder of the values Tyrtaeus had preached: the obligation to die in one’s post rather than retreat. The Spartans were later celebrated with an annual festival at which boys competed in athletic contests, honouring the memory of those who fell. In Roman culture, Horace’s Ode 3.2 — another prescribed literary source — took this Spartan ideal and applied it to Roman citizens: dying for Rome is sweet and fitting, Horace writes, a sentiment that echoes Tyrtaeus across several centuries.

Roman Values of War: Virtue, Duty and Glory

Roman military values overlapped with Greek ones but had their own character. The Latin term virtus meant something like courage combined with excellence of character — the qualities that made a man capable of outstanding action. For Romans, virtus was demonstrated above all in war. A general who won a great victory could be awarded a triumph, the highest military honour: a procession through Rome to the Capitol at which the general rode in a chariot, his face painted red to resemble Jupiter, with his soldiers, captives and plunder parading behind him.

Roman literature also shaped and celebrated military values. Horace’s Ode 3.2, written under Augustus, tells Roman youths to harden themselves to war and endure hardship — the poem praises the man who dies for his country and condemns the coward who tries to live by dishonest means. Virgil’s Aeneid, also written in the Augustan period, presents Aeneas as the model Roman leader: pious, dutiful, restrained, willing to sacrifice personal happiness for the welfare of his people and for the destiny Rome must fulfil.

Key Fact

Roman values of war are expressed in two key literary sources: Horace’s Ode 3.2 praises dying for one’s country and condemns cowardice; Virgil’s Aeneid presents Aeneas as the ideal Roman leader — courageous, dutiful and self-sacrificing. Both poems were written in the reign of Augustus and helped define what Rome stood for.

Greek heroic culture, as expressed by Tyrtaeus, centred on individual honour (kleos, time) and the shame of surviving without it. The Spartan ideal pushed this to an extreme: only death in the front rank was truly honourable; any other outcome was degrading. Roman heroic culture, as expressed by Horace and Virgil, added the idea of collective duty to the state and to Rome’s divine destiny. Aeneas is not simply a brave warrior — he subordinates everything to the divine mission assigned to him. He weeps, suffers and sometimes wishes to die, but his commitment to duty (Latin: pietas) always prevails. This shift from personal glory to public duty is a meaningful difference between Greek and Roman heroic values, though both cultures agreed that the soldier who fought bravely and died well was the highest embodiment of their civic ideal.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing Greek and Roman heroic values, be precise about which sources express which ideas. Tyrtaeus Fragment 10 is Spartan and Greek; Horace Ode 3.2 and the Aeneid are Roman and Augustan. Don’t mix them up. For essay questions asking you to evaluate how far war was ‘glorified’ in the ancient world, remember that the literary sources you are studying were written by educated men for educated audiences — they present an idealised version of war rather than the experience of ordinary soldiers. A strong answer will raise this distinction between ideal and reality.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Greek heroic values (kleos, time) centred on individual glory in battle and the shame of cowardice; Tyrtaeus’s Fragment 10 and the Spartan bronze warrior figure are key sources expressing this ideal.
  • Roman heroic values (virtus, pietas) combined courage with duty to the state; Horace’s Ode 3.2 and Virgil’s Aeneid are the key literary sources, both written to support Augustan ideals.
  • A key difference: Greek heroism focused on personal glory; Roman heroism increasingly emphasised collective duty and the mission of Rome, though both cultures agreed that dying bravely for one’s community was the highest honour.

The response argues that both cultures agreed on the supreme value of dying bravely, but identifies meaningful differences: Greek culture centred on individual glory; Roman culture added collective duty and divine destiny. Named sources are used precisely. A supported conclusion is reached.

practice_questions.text: How effectively did literature glorify war in the ancient Greek and Roman world? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained and nuanced argument evaluating multiple literary sources (Tyrtaeus Fragment 10, Horace Ode 3.2, Virgil Aeneid, Homer Iliad where relevant) against the values they celebrate, considering their different purposes, audiences and contexts. The response also evaluates glorification against depictions of horror, loss and suffering in the same tradition, and considers material evidence (Spartan bronze warrior, war monuments) as a counterpoint. A clear, supported judgement is reached about how effectively and completely literature glorified war — acknowledging that even sources that celebrate heroism often acknowledge its cost.
Secure: A clear argument with relevant evidence from at least three sources. Some balance between glorification and complexity. A supported conclusion.
Developing: Covers two or three sources but argument is underdeveloped or one-sided.
Emerging: Simple points; largely descriptive; limited source use.

lessons.title: The Material Culture of War
lessons.description: How armour, monuments and relief sculpture depicted and idealised war — from the Lenormant relief to Trajan's Column.
lessons.content_html:
Reading War Through Objects and Monuments

The ancient world did not record war only in words. Armour, weapons, coins, sculptural reliefs and triumphal arches were all part of how war was presented, commemorated and made meaningful. These material culture of war tells us things literary sources cannot: how soldiers actually looked, how battles felt to those watching a monument built in their city, and — crucially — how victory was turned into a lasting statement of power. This lesson draws together the main prescribed visual and material sources for ancient warfare.

Helmets, Armour and Identity

Individual pieces of armour are among the most personal of all military artefacts. The Corinthian helmet is the most iconic type associated with Greek hoplite warfare. The prescribed Corinthian helmet in the British Museum (1824, 0407.32), dedicated to Zeus at Olympia around 460 BC, is made of hammered bronze, shaped to cover the entire head and face except for a narrow T-shaped opening for the eyes and mouth. The front was decorated with a sharp nasal guard, and in use a crest of horsehair would have been fitted to the top. The decoration on many Corinthian helmets — serpents, owls, Gorgon faces — was intended both to terrify the enemy and to invoke divine protection.

That this particular helmet was dedicated at Olympia is significant. Victorious athletes and generals dedicated trophies and weapons at major sanctuaries as acts of thanksgiving to the gods. A helmet hung in the sanctuary of Zeus was simultaneously a religious offering and a public advertisement of military success. The object thus functioned in two registers: as a piece of military equipment and as a religious artefact. This dual function is typical of Greek material culture — the boundary between the military and the sacred was always porous.

Key Fact

The Corinthian helmet in the British Museum (1824, 0407.32) dates to around 460 BC and was dedicated to Zeus at Olympia. It is made of hammered bronze with a T-shaped face opening. Its dedication at a sanctuary shows how Greeks combined military success with religious thanksgiving.

The Lenormant Trireme Relief

The Lenormant Trireme relief is a fragment of carved marble originally from the Acropolis at Athens, dating to around 410 BC. The relief shows the side view of a trireme in motion: the three banks of oarsmen are visible in a staggered arrangement, with the oars protruding outwards at different angles. The crew’s physical effort is suggested by the angle and position of the figures, and a helmsman is visible at the stern. The level of detail in the carving gives us direct evidence for how the trireme was crewed and how its three-bank rowing system worked.

The relief is also useful for understanding naval battle tactics. The trireme’s primary weapon was its bronze-sheathed ram at the waterline. In a battle like Salamis (480 BC), Athenian triremes rowed at speed towards enemy vessels and tried to shear off their oars or punch through their hull with the ram. The Lenormant relief, showing the rowers’ arrangement, helps us understand why speed and coordination were so critical: all three banks of rowers had to stroke in precise rhythm, guided by the flute-player and the helmsman, to generate the burst of speed needed for an effective ramming run.

The Lenormant relief is a fragment — it shows only a portion of one side of one ship. It does not show the full crew in action, the complete three-bank arrangement in cross-section, or the conditions below deck. Scholars have debated for decades exactly how many rowers a trireme carried (the standard figure is 170) and precisely how the three banks were arranged at the sides of the hull. The relief provides a crucial visual snapshot but cannot settle all the questions archaeologists and historians still have about trireme design. This is a reminder of a broader truth: all material sources are fragmentary, and we must be honest about what they can and cannot establish.

Battle Scenes in Greek Sculpture

Greek sculptors regularly depicted warfare on temple friezes and pediments. The South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis, now in the British Museum, shows Greeks fighting Persians in a swirling scene of battle. The carving is in high relief — figures project dramatically from the background, their limbs intertwined in combat. A fallen Persian warrior lies beneath an Athenian who strides over him. The composition celebrates Athenian victory, with Greek figures shown as larger and more dynamic than their opponents. The red-figure kylix by the Triptolemos Painter showing a Persian and a Greek fighting is a complementary source — painted pottery gave the same narrative a domestic scale, bringing images of victory into private homes.

Key Fact

Three prescribed material sources relate to Greek warfare: the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike (marble, British Museum — Greeks fighting Persians); the Lenormant Trireme relief (marble, Acropolis — trireme crew at the oars); the Triptolemos Painter kylix (red-figure pot — Persian and Greek in single combat). Each medium — temple relief, architectural fragment, painted vase — presented war to different audiences.

Roman War Monuments and Commemoration

Rome systematised the commemoration of war on a massive public scale. Trajan’s Column, discussed in an earlier lesson, is the most famous example: a 30-metre marble column with a continuous spiral relief recording both Dacian campaigns in over 150 scenes. The Arch of Trajan at Benevento is decorated with relief panels showing the emperor in his dual role as warrior and benefactor. The relief commemorating the battle of Actium in the Vatican Museum offers a sculptural record of that decisive naval battle, depicting ships and combat in a style calculated to glorify Octavian’s victory.

Coins are among the most widely distributed material sources for Roman warfare. The Mark Antony Legionary denarius (minted approximately 32 BC, example in the British Museum BMC 197) has a warship with banners on one face and an eagle between two military standards on the other. This coin was literally struck to pay soldiers before the battle of Actium: it was a wage payment that also served as propaganda, advertising Antony’s fleet and his military strength. The coin type tells us about the relationship between payment, loyalty and military identity in the Roman world — a legionary holding this coin was being told, in miniature, that he was part of a powerful armed force with divine symbols on its side.

Both Greek and Roman visual sources idealise war rather than record it neutrally. Greek temple friezes show Athenians as powerful, upright and victorious over crumpling Persians — this is a political statement, not a documentary record. Roman monuments go further: Trajan’s Column never shows Roman soldiers committing atrocities, looting civilians or running away. The defeated Dacians are shown as brave enemies to make the conquest more impressive, and Trajan himself is always central and commanding. Both traditions use selectivity to project the values their societies most wanted to celebrate — courage, discipline, divine favour and civic virtue. Students who treat these sources as straightforward records will miss half the information they contain.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Source analysis is at the heart of this topic. When you are given a visual source in the exam, identify: (1) what the object is and its medium (marble relief, bronze statuette, red-figure pot, coin); (2) specific details you can see or know about it; (3) what those details reveal about warfare or military values; (4) what the source cannot tell us or how it may be selective or biased. A response that only describes what the object looks like, without moving to analysis and evaluation, will score in the lower bands. Aim to use the phrase “this reveals” or “this suggests” to push yourself from description to analysis.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Key prescribed material sources for Greek warfare include the Corinthian helmet dedicated at Olympia (British Museum), the Lenormant Trireme relief (showing trireme crew), the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike (Greeks vs Persians), and the Triptolemos Painter kylix; each presents war to a different audience and in a different medium.
  • Roman sources — Trajan’s Column, the Arch of Trajan at Benevento, the Actium relief, and the Mark Antony Legionary denarius — systematically glorified Roman military victories and the emperors who won them.
  • All these sources are selective: they present idealised versions of war and must be evaluated critically — what they show, what they choose not to show, and for what audience and purpose they were created.

practice_questions.text: Name one prescribed visual source that provides evidence for naval warfare in ancient Greece.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: the Lenormant Trireme relief (Acropolis relief); the red-figure kylix of a Persian and Greek fighting by the Triptolemos Painter (accept either); the South frieze of the Temple of Athena Nike.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Corinthian helmet dedicated at Olympia (British Museum 1824, 0407.32) and explain what it reveals about Greek military and religious practice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point up to three: the helmet is made of hammered bronze; it covers the entire head and face except for a T-shaped opening for eyes and mouth; it was made around 460 BC; it was dedicated to Zeus at Olympia as a religious offering after a military success; this shows that Greeks combined military victory with religious thanksgiving; dedicating weapons at sanctuaries was a way of publicly advertising military achievement.

practice_questions.text:
Look at this description of a prescribed Greek material source: a fragment of carved marble, approximately 50 cm in length, showing the side view of a large rowing vessel. Three staggered rows of oarsmen are visible, each row set slightly higher than the one below. The oars project outward at different angles, suggesting the ship is in motion. A helmsman figure is faintly visible at one end. The fragment was found on the Acropolis at Athens.

What does this source tell us about naval warfare in ancient Greece? Use specific details from the source in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis linking specific features (three staggered banks of rowers, oars at angles, helmsman position) to wider knowledge of trireme design and tactics (ramming speed requiring coordinated rowing, the role of the helmsman, the arrangement needed for three-bank rowing). The response also evaluates the source's limitations: it is a fragment, it does not show the full ship in cross-section, it shows the ship at rest or gentle rowing rather than in the burst of speed needed for ramming. At least two specific details are used analytically.
Secure: Clear use of specific details with accurate supporting knowledge of the trireme. Some evaluative comment.
Developing: General reference to oarsmen and the trireme; limited use of specific details.
Emerging: Minimal engagement; vague knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Roman monuments were designed to communicate ideas about military power.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each accurate point plus 1 mark for development, up to four marks. Points might include: Trajan's Column placed the narrative of conquest at the heart of the city where every Roman could see it; the Arch of Trajan at Benevento was positioned on a major road so that every traveller was reminded of Roman victory; the continuous spiral narrative on Trajan's Column presented the campaigns as a coherent story of Roman greatness; relief sculpture always showed the emperor in commanding positions; coins spread military imagery to every corner of the empire; these monuments associated the emperor with divine favour and military excellence.

practice_questions.text: How useful are the prescribed material sources for understanding what it was actually like to fight in ancient warfare?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced analysis covering the genuine information provided by material sources (equipment visible on the bronze legionary statuette; rowing system visible on the Lenormant Trireme relief; tactics implied by relief carving) against their fundamental limitations (all are official or elite productions; none show fear, fatigue, death or defeat from the combatant's perspective; all idealise). The response argues that material sources tell us a great deal about how war was presented but much less about how it was experienced by ordinary soldiers. Named sources are used precisely.
Secure: Clear discussion of both uses and limitations, with specific reference to named sources.
Developing: Mainly one-sided; either uncritically values material sources or dismisses them.
Emerging: Vague; limited source knowledge; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text: How effectively do the prescribed material sources present the reality of war in the ancient world? Use a range of evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument engaging with a range of prescribed sources (Corinthian helmet, Lenormant Trireme relief, Temple of Athena Nike frieze, Triptolemos Painter kylix, Trajan's Column, Arch of Trajan, Actium relief, Mark Antony denarius) and evaluating what each reveals and conceals. The response argues that all material sources are selective — they present war through the lens of commemoration, propaganda or religious offering rather than lived experience — but that together they reveal military equipment, tactics, logistics and values with considerable precision. The response considers the difference between Greek and Roman approaches to commemorating war. A supported judgement is reached.
Secure: A clear argument engaging with at least four named sources, weighing their uses and limitations. A supported conclusion.
Developing: Covers two or three sources; limited balance or development.
Emerging: Simple points; largely descriptive; few named sources.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical objects, art and architecture through which a society expresses, records and transmits its experiences and values; in classical studies, this includes weapons, coins, sculpture and monuments.
A type of Greek helmet with a protective guard covering the cheeks and nasal, leaving only a narrow T-shaped opening; widely used from the seventh to fifth century BC.
A marble relief from the Acropolis of Athens showing the crew of a trireme warship at their oars; one of the best material sources for understanding how the trireme was operated.
A Greek painted drinking cup decorated with figures left in the natural red colour of the clay against a black-painted background; used widely for narrative scenes of myth and everyday life.
